summary: Inside the empty tomb, angels tell the women that Jesus is risen, as He said. They flee trembling, then tell the apostles, who dismiss their words as idle tales.
key_insight: In all three accounts the angels point back to Jesus’ own words: “as He said” (Matthew), “as He said to you” (Mark), “Remember how He spoke to you” (Luke). The resurrection was not a new announcement. It was a promise kept.
story: Inside the tomb the women were greatly perplexed, and suddenly two men in shining garments stood by them. {Lk} Mark describes the one who spoke as a young man clothed in a long white robe, sitting on the right side, and the women were alarmed. {Mk} In fear they bowed their faces to the earth. {Lk}
The angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for He is risen, as He said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.” {Mt}

“Why do you seek the living among the dead?” they asked. “Remember how He spoke to you when He was still in Galilee, saying, ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again.’ ” And they remembered His words. {Lk}

Then the angel sent them: “And go quickly and tell His disciples that He is risen from the dead, and indeed He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see Him.” {Mt} Mark records that the message named one disciple in particular: “and Peter.” {Mk}
The women went out quickly and fled from the tomb, for they trembled and were amazed. “And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” {Mk}

They returned from the tomb and told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles. But “their words seemed to them like idle tales, and they did not believe them.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew speaks of an angel, Mark of a young man in a long white robe, Luke of two men in shining garments.
In Mark the young man is sitting on the right side inside the tomb; in Luke the two men stand by the women; Matthew earlier had the angel sitting on the stone (28:2).
Only Mark adds “and Peter.” Only Luke asks, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” and tells that the women remembered Jesus’ words.
Matthew and Mark give the promise of meeting Jesus in Galilee; Luke speaks instead of what Jesus said while He was still in Galilee.
Mark ends with the women fleeing in fear and saying “nothing to anyone.” Luke says they told the eleven and all the rest, names Joanna among them, and adds that the apostles did not believe them.

fit.question: Was there one angel (Matthew and Mark) or two (Luke)? Was he sitting (Mark), or were they standing (Luke)? And was the angel on the stone outside (Matthew) or inside the tomb (Mark)?

points.label: The one who spoke
points.text: Matthew and Mark tell of the angel who spoke. Luke, and John at the tomb later that morning (John 20:12), mention two. Saying that an angel spoke is not saying that only one was there, just as Matthew counts two blind men at Jericho where Mark and Luke tell of one (event 127).

points.label: Men in appearance
points.text: Angels in Scripture often appear as men; Luke himself describes the angels at the ascension as “two men” in white (Acts 1:10). Mark’s “young man” and Luke’s “two men” describe how they looked. Luke later calls them angels (Luke 24:23).

points.label: Sitting and standing, outside and in
points.text: Luke’s word for “stood by them” is often used of someone suddenly appearing, as when an angel of the Lord “stood before” the shepherds (Luke 2:9). Matthew’s angel sat on the stone when he rolled it away, before the women came (28:2); when he speaks, he invites them to “come, see the place where the Lord lay” (28:6), and Mark places him inside. In a scene of a few moments, place and posture can change.

fit.note: All three report the same heavenly message. Differences in the number and posture of the messengers are the kind honest witnesses leave unsmoothed.
fit.short: Two angels were there; Matthew and Mark mention the one who spoke. Luke’s “stood” means appeared, and place and posture can change in a moment.

fit.question: Mark says the women fled and “said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” Luke says they told all these things to the eleven, and Matthew says they ran to bring the disciples word (Matthew 28:8). Did the women keep silent or tell the disciples?

points.label: Silent on the way
points.text: Mark uses the same kind of phrase when Jesus told the cleansed leper, “See that you say nothing to anyone; but go your way, show yourself to the priest” (Mark 1:44). The leper was to tell no one along the way, yet report to the priest. The women likewise spoke to no one as they fled, until they reached the disciples.

points.label: Fear first, then the report
points.text: Their fear may also have held them for a time. Matthew says they went “with fear and great joy,” and that Jesus Himself met them and said, “Do not be afraid. Go and tell My brethren” (Matthew 28:10; event 180). After that they told the eleven.

points.label: Luke sums up the morning
points.text: Luke gathers the women’s reports into one sentence and names Mary Magdalene among them. He does not track who told what, or when; John shows that Mary brought her own reports to the disciples separately (John 20:2, 18).

fit.note: Mark describes the women’s fearful silence as they fled; Matthew and Luke describe the report they then gave the disciples. Both are true of the same frightened, joyful morning.
fit.short: They told no one along the way, then reported to the disciples, as Matthew and Luke say. Mark’s “say nothing to anyone” fits Mark 1:44.

scene.label: The living among the dead
scene.text: Tombs were places of the dead, and the law made anyone who touched a grave unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). The angels’ question tells the women they have come to the wrong place to look for Jesus.

scene.label: Galilee
scene.text: On the way to the Mount of Olives after the Last Supper, Jesus had said, “But after I have been raised, I will go before you to Galilee” (Matthew 26:32; Mark 14:28). The angel repeats the promise. Most of the disciples were Galileans, and there the risen Jesus would meet them on a mountain (Matthew 28:16).

scene.label: Words spoken in Galilee
scene.text: Luke records Jesus foretelling His death and rising during His Galilean ministry (Luke 9:22) and again on the road to Jerusalem (18:31–33). The disciples did not understand; Luke says “this saying was hidden from them” (18:34).

scene.label: “Idle tales”
scene.text: Luke’s word, used only here in the New Testament, means nonsense or empty talk. The apostles were not waiting to believe in a resurrection. Later that day two disciples spoke of the women’s report as something that had astonished them, not as news they believed (Luke 24:22–24).

witnesses.matthew: Matthew’s angel invites the women, “Come, see the place where the Lord lay,” and then sends them: “go quickly and tell.” In Matthew the heavenly message points straight to Galilee, where his Gospel ends with the risen King sending His disciples to all the nations (28:16–20).
witnesses.mark: Mark alone records “and Peter,” and early tradition held that his Gospel carries Peter’s own memories; if so, Peter told how the first message from the risen Lord singled out by name the disciple who had denied Him. Mark alone also says the women fled trembling and “said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.” In some of the oldest manuscripts, Mark’s Gospel ends with these words (see event 179).
witnesses.luke: Luke’s angels ask why the women seek the living among the dead and call them to remember Jesus’ words. Luke alone names Joanna among the women who carried the news and records that the apostles took it as “idle tales.” For Luke the resurrection fulfills what Jesus said “must” happen, a theme that returns at the end of the chapter (24:44).

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ word proved true to the letter: delivered, crucified, and risen on the third day. The risen Lord also kept His promise to go before His disciples, including the one who had denied Him.
seeing.living: The women understood when they remembered His words. Doubt often grows from forgetting what Jesus has said rather than from lack of evidence. Go back to His words, and let them explain what you see.
seeing.ponder: Where are you still seeking the living Jesus among the dead?

preaching.big_idea: He is not here; He is risen, just as He said.
outline: A report dismissed as idle tales (9–11)
preaching.watch_for: Luke’s word “must” (v. 7) runs through Jesus’ predictions (9:22; 22:37) and returns in His own words that evening: “all things must be fulfilled” (24:44). The cross and the empty tomb were God’s plan, not an accident.
